syllabus.clause: a topic is divided into partitions, each an ordered append-only log, so ordering is scoped to a partition, not the topic. Key-based partitioning (hash(key) % N) preserves per-key order while spreading load, and changing N breaks it. Segment files and sparse offset indexes.

at.step: Measured: every one of many writes to the same key genuinely landed in the identical partition, in the identical order it was written
Measured: changing the partition count genuinely rerouted at least one existing key to a different partition
Measured: the rerouted key's own history genuinely split across the old and the new partition; the order guarantee it had is genuinely gone

items.item: topics are broken up into partitions, meaning a single topic log is broken into multiple logs located on different Kafka brokers

at.step: A topic's writes, for many different keys, go through one real partitioning function, hash of the key modulo the partition count. Does every write to the same key genuinely always land in the same partition?

items.item: events with the same event key are written to the same partition, and any consumer of a given topic partition will always read that partition's events in exactly the same order as they were written

at.step: Confluent's own documentation states this exact mechanism directly: events with the same key are written to the same partition, and a consumer of a given partition always reads it in exactly the order it was written. Does this topic's own code measure exactly that rule?

items.item: events with the same key are written to the same partition; both producers can write to the same partition if appropriate

items.item: the message log maintained by the broker is itself just a directory of files, each populated by a sequence of message sets that have been written to disk in the same format used by the producer and consumer

at.step: The Kafka project's own design document describes the message log itself as just a directory of real files on disk, recopied in whole segments whenever the log cleaner compacts it. Does this topic's own partition-per-vector model mirror that same real, append-only shape?

items.item: log compaction is handled by the log cleaner, a pool of background threads that recopy log segment files, removing records whose key appears in the head of the log

items.item: The partitioning function used here (FNV-1a over the key's own bytes, then modulo the partition count) is a plain, deterministic string hash rather than Rust's own std DefaultHasher, specifically because std's own hasher output is explicitly not guaranteed stable across Rust versions; a toy meant to measure a real, repeatable routing rule needs a hash whose output never silently changes under it.

at.step: A topic's writes, for many different keys, go through one real partitioning function, hash of the key modulo the partition count. Does every write to the same key genuinely always land in the same partition?

items.item: The fixed-partition-count scenario writes twenty interleaved rounds across five distinct keys rather than twenty consecutive writes to one key, so the measured per-key order guarantee is checked against real interleaving with other keys' own writes, not an artificially simplified single-key stream.

at.step: Measured: every one of many writes to the same key genuinely landed in the identical partition, in the identical order it was written

items.item: The resize scenario keeps the already-written entries in their own original partition rather than replaying the whole log under the new partition count, since this mirrors how a real partitioned log actually behaves on a resize: existing segments stay exactly where they already are, and only new writes are routed by the new count.

at.step: That rerouted key keeps writing after the resize. Does its own history now genuinely live in one partition, or does it genuinely split?

items.item: The measured claim that a rerouted key's history splits is checked by asserting the exact entry count in both the old and the new partition after the resize, not merely that the two partition indices differ; this rules out a routing function that happens to compute a different index but still somehow leaves the key's entries untouched.

at.step: Measured: the rerouted key's own history genuinely split across the old and the new partition; the order guarantee it had is genuinely gone

items.item: The partition count change used here (four partitions growing to six) is a real, concrete case chosen because it is guaranteed to reroute at least one of the five sample keys under FNV-1a, which the code itself locates and asserts on, rather than assuming a reroute happens without checking for one.
